section.title: The New Jerusalem
section.sectionRationale: Where 21:1-8 declared the new creation in overview from the throne, one of the seven bowl angels now carries John away for a guided, measured tour of the bride city itself. The unit is bounded by the angel's invitation, 'Come, I will show you the bride,' and closes with the vision's own resolution, no more curse, unbroken worship, and an eternal reign, before the epilogue's final words begin in 22:6. It is the single most sustained description of the eternal state in Scripture, and it forms one coherent scene of showing and measuring.
section.thesis: The bride, the holy city, descends in full splendor, gathering up temple, garden, and city imagery at once: no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple; no curse, because the tree of life stands open again; and no night, because the Lord God is its everlasting light.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the bride, the holy city, shown descending in glory with its named gates and foundations; the angel measuring the city's dimensions and cataloguing its gold, gems, and pearls; the declaration that there is no temple and no night, because God and the Lamb are the city's temple and lamp; the river of the water of life and the tree of life flowing from the throne; and the closing promise of no more curse, unbroken worship, and an everlasting reign.

verses.text: Then one of the seven angels with the seven bowls full of the seven final plagues came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the {{nymphe|bride}}, the wife of the Lamb.”
And he carried me away in the Spirit to a mountain great and high, and showed me the holy city of Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God,
shining with the glory of God. Its radiance was like a most precious jewel, like a jasper, as clear as crystal.
The city had a great and high wall with twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, and twelve angels at the gates.
There were three gates on the east, three on the north, three on the south, and three on the west.
The wall of the city had twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

units.label: Measuring the city of gold and jewels
units.note: a golden rod, a perfect cube

verses.text: The angel who spoke with me had a golden measuring rod to measure the city and its gates and walls.
The city lies foursquare, with its width the same as its length. And he measured the city with the rod, and all its dimensions were equal: 12,000 stadia in length and width and height.
And he measured its wall to be 144 cubits, by the human measure the angel was using.
The wall was made of jasper, and the city itself of pure gold, as pure as glass.
The foundations of the city walls were adorned with every kind of precious stone: the first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald,
the fifth sardonyx, the sixth carnelian, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, and the twelfth amethyst.
And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, with each gate consisting of a single pearl. The main street of the city was pure gold, as clear as glass.

units.label: No temple, for God and the Lamb are its temple

verses.text: But I saw no {{naos|temple}} in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its {{naos|temple}}.
And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp.
By its light the nations will walk, and into it the kings of the earth will bring their glory.
Its gates will never be shut at the end of the day, because there will be no night there.
And into the city will be brought the glory and honor of the nations.
But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who practices an abomination or a lie, but only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life.

units.label: The river and the tree of life

verses.text: Then the angel showed me a river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb

down the middle of the main street of the city. On either side of the river stood a {{xylon_zoes|tree of life}}, bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.

units.label: No more curse, they will reign forever

verses.text: No longer will there be any {{katathema|curse}}. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be within the city, and His servants will {{latreuo|worship}} Him.
They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads.
There will be no more night in the city, and they will have no need for the light of a lamp or of the sun. For the Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever.

nymphe.gloss: Bride, or young wife. The church is shown as the bride, the wife of the Lamb, the consummation of the marriage supper announced in Revelation 19:7-9. It gathers up the covenant marriage imagery used of Israel and the church throughout Scripture into one final, descending city.

naos.gloss: The inner sanctuary or temple proper, the innermost dwelling place of God, distinct from the wider temple courts. Its total absence here is itself the fulfillment: God and the Lamb are the naos, so there is no longer any localized, separate sanctuary, only unmediated presence filling the whole city.

xylon_zoes.gloss: Tree of life, xylon meaning wood or tree, zoes the genitive of life. It recalls the tree of Genesis 2:9, once guarded from fallen humanity by a flaming sword, now standing open on both sides of the river, its leaves given for healing rather than judgment.

katathema.gloss: An accursed or banned thing, a word related to anathema. It is distinct from katara, the more common New Testament word for curse used, for example, in Galatians 3:13. Its complete absence here declares the reversal of the curse placed on the ground and on humanity in Genesis 3:17-19.

latreuo.gloss: To render priestly service or worship, the word used throughout the Greek Old Testament for Israel's tabernacle and temple service. Here it names the unbroken, priestly worship of God's servants who see His face directly, distinct from proskyneo, to bow down, though both belong to the redeemed.

basic.context: An angel carries John to a high mountain to show him the bride, the holy city, descending from heaven in dazzling glory. He measures its walls, gates, and foundations, all named for the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles, built of gold, jewels, and pearl.
basic.hermeneutics: Readers debate whether the city's exact measurements and jewels describe a literal building or are rich symbols, especially since the city is a perfect cube, the same shape as the Holy of Holies in Solomon's temple. Either way, the point is clear: full, ordered, priestly access to God for His whole people forever.
basic.originalLanguages: The bride, nymphe, is the church, the wife of the Lamb. There is no naos, temple, because God and the Lamb are the temple. The xylon zoes, tree of life, once barred, now grows freely, and there is no more katathema, curse, only unbroken latreuo, worship.
basic.typology: The tree of life barred in Eden is freely accessible again; the whole city is shaped like the Most Holy Place, once entered only once a year by one priest; and the bride city fulfills the marriage covenant God made with His people from Hosea to Ephesians.
basic.christ: The Lamb shares the very throne of God, is the city's lamp and its temple, and is Bridegroom to the bride shown here; His name is written on His people's foreheads, and it is by His blood, named just before this vision, that anyone's name stands in the Book of Life.
basic.god: God and the Lamb together are the city's light, its temple, and its throne; His unmediated presence, once approached only through priest, veil, and blood, is now the whole city's atmosphere, and His people will see His face and reign with Him forever.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 6:20 describes the cube-shaped Holy of Holies. Exodus 28:17-21 lists the twelve jewels of the priestly breastpiece. Isaiah 60 promises nations walking by Zion's light and kings bringing their glory. Genesis 2-3 is the tree of life and the curse this vision reverses.
basic.oneStory: Eden had one tree of life, barred by a flaming sword and cherubim after the fall. Here the tree grows freely on both sides of a river flowing straight from God's throne, and there is no more curse at all, the ancient exile fully and finally undone.

context.literary:
The tour of the city is built on a pattern of showing and measuring. It opens with the invitation of 21:9, 'Come, I will show you the bride,' and it closes in 22:5 with the city shining without any lamp. The angel is the same sort of guide who opened the vision of Babylon in 17:1, one of the seven with the bowls, and the Spirit again carries John away, this time to 'a mountain great and high,' 21:10, as Ezekiel was set down on a very high mountain to see a city in Ezekiel 40:2. Where John saw a woman on a beast in a wilderness, he now sees a woman as a city on a mountain. The two cities are set side by side, and every reader is asked which one they live in.

The description moves from the outside in. First the radiance, then the wall and its twelve gates, with their names and angels, then the foundations, then the measuring, then the materials, then the interior, where there is no temple, no sun and no night, and finally the river and the tree, which stand in the middle of the street. The movement is toward the centre, and the centre is the throne, 22:1. Verses 22 to 27 of chapter 21 are a series of negatives that describe what the city does not need, a temple, sun, moon, a shut gate, night, or anything unclean. The final sentences of 22:1 to 5 turn them into positives, a river, a tree, a face, a name and a reign.

The passage is full of twelves. Twelve gates, twelve angels, twelve tribes, twelve foundations, twelve apostles, twelve stones, twelve pearls, twelve kinds of fruit, and 12,000 stadia on each side. The wall is 144 cubits, which is twelve times twelve. The effect is of fullness and completeness, and it ties the vision to the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles, and so to the whole people of God. The chapter division is unhelpful here, since 22:1 to 5 belongs to the vision that began in 21:9, and the end of the vision at 22:5 repeats 'no more night' from 21:25 as a frame around the whole.
context.historical:
For a first-century believer, Jerusalem meant the temple, and the temple had been destroyed by Rome. Whether John wrote before or after AD 70, the hearers knew what a city without a temple would sound like, and what a city built to the dimensions of the Most Holy Place would mean. In Solomon's temple the inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, wide and high and overlaid with pure gold, 1 Kings 6:19-20. John's city is a cube, 'pure gold, as pure as glass,' and the high priest alone could enter such a room, once a year, Hebrews 9:7. The city is a shrine large enough for all the people.

The jewels evoked the high priest's breastpiece, with twelve stones for the twelve tribes, Exodus 28:17-21, though the lists are not the same in order or in name, and the prophets had imagined a rebuilt Zion with sapphire foundations and gates of jewels, Isaiah 54:11-12. The gates, three on each side and named for the tribes, follow Ezekiel's vision of a restored city, Ezekiel 48:30-34. In the cities John's readers knew, the gate was where the elders sat, where trade was done and where armies were kept out. A gate that is never shut by day or night in 21:25 would have sounded like perfect peace in a world of walls and watchmen.

The 12,000 stadia, about 1,380 miles by the BSB footnote, is far larger than any city of the ancient world, and Rome at its height was a tiny fraction of the size. Readers who knew the great cities of the Mediterranean would have seen the point at once. The new city dwarfs the empire's capital, and it has no need of an army, a harbour or a market. The kings who bring 'their glory' also echo the picture of Isaiah 60 and Psalm 72:10-11, where the nations come to Zion with their wealth, but now they come to a city whose light is the Lamb.
context.canonical:
Almost every phrase here is borrowed and then raised. Ezekiel 40 to 48 is the largest source: the very high mountain, the measuring, the gates named for the tribes, the river flowing from the temple with trees on both banks whose fruit comes every month and whose leaves are for healing, Ezekiel 47:12, and the final name of the city, 'THE LORD IS THERE,' Ezekiel 48:35. John's river and tree take Ezekiel's picture and remove the temple from which it flowed. The river now comes straight 'from the throne of God and of the Lamb,' 22:1.

Isaiah 60 supplies the nations and the light. 'Nations will come to your light,' Isaiah 60:3, 'Your gates will always stand open,' Isaiah 60:11, and 'the LORD will be your everlasting light,' 60:19-20. The tree and the river go further back, to Genesis 2:9-10, where a river flowed out of Eden and the tree of life stood in the middle of the garden, and to Psalm 46:4, 'There is a river whose streams delight the city of God.' Zechariah 14:8 promises living water flowing out of Jerusalem, and 14:11 promises that 'never again will there be an utter destruction,' the sentence John renders as 'no longer will there be any curse.'

The New Testament has been preparing the reader. Paul speaks of 'the Jerusalem above,' Galatians 4:26, and Hebrews says that Abraham looked for 'the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God,' Hebrews 11:10, and that believers have already come to 'the heavenly Jerusalem,' Hebrews 12:22. Ephesians 2:19-22 describes the church as a household built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, which is why the foundations carry the apostles' names. The bride of Revelation 19:7-8 and the promise of Revelation 3:12, that the overcomer will bear the name of the city of God, are fulfilled when the angel says, 'I will show you the bride.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wanted believers who were poor and pressed to see what they were being kept for, and to see it as a city rather than as a feeling. The long catalogue of gold, pearl and jasper is not meant to make them love luxury. In a world where those materials were symbols of Rome's wealth, he takes them and lays them under the feet of the redeemed, so that the empire's gold becomes the paving of the street. The splendour that Babylon imitated is the real thing here.

He also wanted them to feel the ease of access. For people who knew that only a single priest could enter the Holy of Holies, the picture of a whole people who live in that room, who see God's face and who bear His name where the high priest bore it, would have been astounding. The throne is in the city, the river runs from it, and the servants worship Him.

And he wanted the vision to shape their present. The nations walk by the light, the kings bring their glory, and the gates are not shut, so there is room for people from every corner of the earth. Yet nothing unclean enters, so the call to be among those 'whose names are written in the Lamb's Book of Life,' 21:27, is real. The vision is an invitation to be faithful now, and the hearers are meant to refuse Babylon, whose lights and voices will be heard no more, Revelation 18:23, and to keep their eyes on the lamp of the Lamb.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes the eternal state and gives no instructions about building anything. The city is not a plan for a Christian architecture or a church of gold, and it is not a code from which dates or dimensions can be calculated. The measuring is done by the angel, and the human reader is asked only to look.

What it prescribes is carried in two verses. The first is the list of verse 27, which presses the reader to belong to the Lamb's book. The second is the implied command of 22:3 to worship, since the city is a place of service and sight. The present church is already described as a temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16, and as a royal priesthood, 1 Peter 2:9, so these verses show where that calling ends rather than make a new one. Believers practise now what they will do then, which is to worship God and the Lamb, to see Him by faith, and to live in the light.

debates.question: Are the New Jerusalem's measurements, 12,000 stadia and 144 cubits, and its jewels literal architecture, or symbolic of something else?

views.label: A literal, physical city of these dimensions
views.case: John records precise numbers, taken with an actual measuring rod, as one would expect of a real described place. The BSB footnote gives about 1,380 miles on each side. Those who read it literally point out that the new heaven and earth of 21:1 are a real creation, so a real city within it is not odd, and that Hebrews 11:10 speaks of a city with foundations that God Himself builds.

views.label: Rich symbolism drawn from the Holy of Holies and the twelve tribes and apostles
views.case: The city is a perfect cube, the shape of the Most Holy Place in 1 Kings 6:20, and everything in it is a multiple of twelve, 12 gates, 12 foundations, 144 cubits and 12,000 stadia. On this reading the numbers say that the whole city is one vast sanctuary and that the whole people of God, tribes and apostles together, live in it. John has also called the city a bride, 21:9, which is plainly not a building, and the gates of pearl and streets of transparent gold are not meant to be pictured at engineering scale.

views.label: Both a place and a people
views.case: Some hold that the city is a real dwelling and that it is simultaneously the people, since the bride and the city are the same figure in 21:9 and 21:10, and since the apostles' names stand in its foundations. The book often joins symbol and reality, as with the Lamb who is also a lion in 5:5-6.

debates.bearing: The central claim survives all three readings: God lives with His people, completely and for ever, without a veil. The reader is saved from both over-reading, as if the numbers could be added up into a chart, and under-reading, as though the city were a pretty picture without substance.

debates.question: Who are the 'nations' and 'kings of the earth' who walk by the city's light, and how does that fit the exclusion of the unclean?

views.label: The redeemed from every nation
views.case: Revelation 5:9 and 7:9 speak of people purchased from every tribe and tongue and nation, and 21:24 and 22:2 name the same nations as those who live by the city's light and are healed by the tree. The 'kings' are believers who reign, 1:6 and 22:5. Nothing needs to be added to the gathered saints.

views.label: Nations that survive judgment and are brought in
views.case: Because the kings of the earth were struck down in 19:18-21, some argue that the kings of 21:24 must be a different group, the nations of the world who remain and are drawn into the city. They note Isaiah 60:3 and 60:11 and read 'the healing of the nations' as a work that continues.

views.label: A universal salvation
views.case: A few read the gates that are never shut as a sign that even those outside will at last come in. Others answer that the same chapter says nothing unclean will 'ever' enter and lists those outside in 22:15, so the open gates are open to everyone who is willing and are never closed on those who wash their robes, 22:14.

debates.bearing: The open gates are real and the boundary is real, and John holds them together. The nations come in with their glory, and the unclean do not. The city is the home of every people who belong to the Lamb, and its gates are an invitation to all who will come.

study.originalLanguages:
The angel's rod measures by 'a human measure, which is an angel's,' as the Greek has it, and the BSB renders it 'by the human measure the angel was using,' verse 17. The odd phrase says that heaven's dimensions are given in a scale humans can read, so John is not describing the city in angelic units that would be beyond him. The city 'lies foursquare,' tetragonos, a word for a square or a cube, and the cube of verse 16 is an unusual shape for an ancient city, which was normally laid out as a rectangle or a circle.

The emphatic negative in 21:25 is the Greek construction ou me, the strongest way to say 'never,' so the gates will 'by no means' be shut. Verse 27 uses the same construction for the unclean who will never enter. The same phrase therefore guards the open gate and the closed door, and John makes the openness and the boundary equally firm. The word for 'unclean' in verse 27 is koinon, literally 'common,' the word Peter used for food that Jewish law counted as common or unclean in Acts 10:14. Here it names whatever is outside the holiness of God.

The word for 'healing' in 22:2, therapeia, is the root of the English 'therapy.' It can also mean service, as when a household is waited on. That fits a tree that nourishes and restores the nations, and it gives the nations' healing a gentle and personal ring. The Greek for 'tree,' xylon, is literally 'wood,' and it is the same word used of the cross in Acts 5:30 and 1 Peter 2:24, a verbal link that is easy to miss in English. The phrase is not an allegory but a quiet echo that the tree of life stands in the new city because of the tree on which Christ was hung.

In 22:3 the word 'curse,' katathema, is rare. The thought behind it is that of Zechariah 14:11, where the Hebrew word cherem, a ban of destruction, will never again fall on Jerusalem. Then comes a detail that is easy to miss: 'His servants will worship Him.' The verb and the pronoun are singular, one 'Him,' though the throne belongs to God and the Lamb. In the same way verse 4 says 'His face' and 'His name,' one face and one name. The Greek treats God and the Lamb as sharing a single throne and a single presence.

The promise 'they will reign forever and ever,' 22:5, has no stated object, and the Greek leaves the verb alone. John does not say what they reign over. The line connects to 1:6, 5:10 and 20:4-6, where those who belong to Christ are called kings and priests, and it suggests that the reign is a share in the Lamb's own rule rather than a rule over anyone else. The phrase 'for ever and ever,' eis tous aionas ton aionon, is the strongest way Greek expresses unending time, and it is the same expression used of the worship of God in 5:13.

typology.fulfillment: The inner sanctuary was a cube of twenty cubits overlaid with pure gold, and the ark of the covenant sat in it, hidden behind a veil. Only the high priest entered it, once a year and never without blood, Leviticus 16:2 and Hebrews 9:7. John's city is a cube of pure gold, and the whole people dwell in it. The escalation comes through Christ, who opened the way through the curtain of His body, Hebrews 10:19-20. The type falls short because the old room held a mercy seat, a piece of furniture, while the new city is simply filled with the One who sat above it.

typology.type: The river and the tree of Eden, Genesis 2:9-10
typology.fulfillment: A river flowed out of Eden and the tree of life stood in the middle of the garden. After the fall the way to that tree was barred, Genesis 3:24. Ezekiel saw a river flow from the temple with trees whose leaves healed, Ezekiel 47:12. In Revelation 22:1-2 the river comes straight from the throne and the tree is on both banks. The garden has become a city without losing its life. The tree is now freely available to those who wash their robes, 22:14, because the Lamb has dealt with the sin that closed the way. The type falls short since Eden's tree was in a single garden, but the new tree heals the nations.

typology.type: The high priest's plate and the name on the forehead, Exodus 28:36-38
typology.fulfillment: Aaron wore on his forehead a plate engraved 'HOLY TO THE LORD,' so that he could bear the iniquity of the holy gifts. In Revelation 22:4 God's name is on the foreheads of His servants, as it was on the 144,000 in 14:1. What belonged to one man now marks a whole people, whom Christ has made 'priests to His God and Father,' Revelation 1:6 and 1 Peter 2:9. The escalation is that the priestly office is shared by all. The type falls short in that Aaron's plate had to cover sin, while this people stands in the face of God with nothing to cover.

typology.type: The twelve tribes and the apostles in gates and foundations, Ezekiel 48:30-34
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel's restored city had twelve gates named for the tribes of Israel, and Revelation 21:12 has the same gates with the names of the tribes. The wall also stands on foundations that carry 'the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb,' 21:14. The two names together show a single people, Israel and the church, one household built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Ephesians 2:19-20. The type falls short in the old covenant, which kept Gentiles at the court's edge, while the nations now walk by the light of this city.

typology.type: Babylon and Babel, the city built without God, Genesis 11:4
typology.fulfillment: At Babel humanity said, 'let us build for ourselves a city,' to make a name for themselves, Genesis 11:4. Revelation 17 and 18 show Babylon at the end of that road, a harlot city of luxury that falls in a single hour, 18:10. The New Jerusalem is the opposite, a city that comes down from God and is built by Him, Hebrews 11:10. Babylon's lamps and wedding voices are gone for ever, 18:23, and the Lamb is the lamp of the bride. The type shows that human cities are not wrong, and that the answer to a corrupted city is a city given by God.

study.christ:
The city is the Lamb's city in nearly every verse. The bride is 'the wife of the Lamb,' the foundations carry the names of 'the apostles of the Lamb,' the Lamb is the temple and the lamp, the throne is 'of God and of the Lamb,' and the Book of Life is 'the Lamb's.' John never lets the reader forget that the one who sits at the centre of this city entered it as a slain Lamb, Revelation 5:6. The title for a conqueror in 5:5 is the Lion of Judah and the Root of David, and what John actually sees is a Lamb. Everything in the city is there because of Him.

He is the temple. In John's Gospel Jesus says, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' and the evangelist adds that 'Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body,' John 2:19-21. The place where heaven and earth were joined in Israel is now a person, and in the city there is no longer any need of a building, because the person is there. He is also the lamp. 'I am the light of the world,' He said in John 8:12, and Isaiah 60:19 had promised that the LORD would be Zion's everlasting light. Revelation puts the two together by calling the Lamb the lamp, and the glory of God the light that the lamp holds.

He opens the way to the tree. The word for tree here is the word for the wood on which He hung, Acts 5:30, and Paul says that He became a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. That is why the verse that follows the tree says 'No longer will there be any curse,' 22:3. The curse of Genesis 3 was borne at a tree so that this tree could feed the nations. The blessing of 22:14, 'Blessed are those who wash their robes,' belongs to the same logic, since the robes are washed in His blood, 7:14.

He is the bridegroom. Paul says that Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her 'to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle,' Ephesians 5:25-27, and the angel's invitation to see the bride is the moment that promise is carried out. The bride has been made ready, 19:7-8, and the groom who made her ready receives her.

And He shares the name. Jesus had promised the overcomer that He would write on him the name of God and the name of the city of God, Revelation 3:12, and in 22:4 the name is on every forehead. The one who bears His name also bears His face, since 'they will see His face,' and John writes that in the singular, one face for God and the Lamb together. The promise of Jesus in John 14:3, 'that you also may be where I am,' comes to its full realisation in a place where He is the centre.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who is the light and the glory of His people. The city has no need of sun or moon because 'the glory of God illuminates the city,' and Isaiah's promise that the LORD Himself would be the everlasting light is carried out in full, Isaiah 60:19. It also points to a God whose presence was once dangerous. Moses was told, 'You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live,' Exodus 33:20, and Paul says that He 'dwells in unapproachable light,' 1 Timothy 6:16. Revelation 22:4 says 'They will see His face.' The God who was hidden for the sake of sinners is now seen by people whom He has made fit to see Him, as Jesus promised the pure in heart, Matthew 5:8, and John writes that 'we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is,' 1 John 3:2.

He is holy, and He is also generous. The city is a Holy of Holies, a place of perfect purity where nothing unclean can come, 21:27. Yet the gates are open all day and there is no night, so the holiness is no reason for anxiety among those who belong. The two are not in tension, because the same God provides the means by which people are made clean. The Lamb's blood washes the robes, 22:14, and the Lamb's book names the citizens, 21:27.

He is the God of the whole creation. The nations come in with their glory and honour, 21:24-26, and the tree heals them. A God who cares only for a few would not set the healing of the nations on the main street of His city. The reach of His kindness matches the reach of His rule, and the worship of the book ends with praise from every creature, Revelation 5:13.

He is the God who keeps His word to the last detail. The promise that was spoken to Abraham, to Moses, to David and to the prophets is gathered here, and the promises of the temple, the land, the tree and the nations are all kept. The unity of the God of the Old Testament with the God of the Lamb is seen in the single throne, the singular 'Him,' and the shared glory.

For worship, the passage invites believers to rest in an end that is entirely given by God. There is no temple to build because He is the temple, no lamp to light because He is the light. The proper response is the one the servants of 22:3 make, which is to serve and worship, and to let that be the shape of life now.

crossReferences.note: Solomon's inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, wide and high, overlaid with pure gold, and it held the ark. The shape explains the equal length, width and height of Revelation 21:16, and the gold of verse 18 and verse 21. The whole city is a room of God's presence, open to all His people.

The high priest's breastpiece carried twelve gemstones, one for each tribe of Israel, set in gold. The jewels in the foundations of the city draw on the same picture, although the lists are not identical, and show that the whole people now carry what was once carried by one man into the presence of God.

Ezekiel's new city has twelve gates named for the tribes, three on each side, and it ends with the name 'THE LORD IS THERE.' Revelation 21:12-13 follows the plan and then makes it new by also naming apostles, and by taking away the temple, since the Lord is now there in person.

Trees on both banks of the river bear fruit each month, and their leaves are for healing, because the water comes from the sanctuary. Revelation 22:2 repeats the monthly fruit and the healing leaves, but the water now comes from the throne, so the sanctuary and the source are one.

The first garden had a river flowing out of Eden and the tree of life in the middle. The last city has the river of the water of life and the tree on either side, so that the end of the Bible is matched to the beginning. What was lost in Genesis 3 is given back in the form of a city.

Isaiah calls Zion to arise and shine, because the LORD's glory rises on her and nations come to her light. Revelation 21:23-24 applies this to the city, where the glory of God is the light and the nations walk by it, and kings bring their glory.

The sun will no longer be Zion's light by day, nor the moon her light by night, for the LORD will be her everlasting light. Revelation 21:23 and 22:5 take the promise word for word in substance, and add the Lamb to it as the lamp.

Living water flows out of Jerusalem, summer and winter, and the city will dwell securely, never again facing utter destruction. Revelation 22:1-3 takes these pictures, the water and the end of the ban of destruction, and gives them the ultimate form of a river from the throne and no curse.

The church is a household built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone, growing into a holy temple. Revelation 21:14 gives the foundations the apostles' names, and the temple of Paul's image becomes the whole city, in which the Lord and the Lamb are the temple.

The readers of Hebrews are told that they have already come to 'the heavenly Jerusalem,' the city of the living God. It shows that the city John sees is not wholly future. The church already belongs to it, and the vision shows what that membership will become.

The same sort of angel with a bowl carries John away in the Spirit to see the great prostitute, and then in 21:9-10 carries him away to see the bride. The deliberate echo asks the reader to compare the two women and the two cities, and to choose which one to belong to.

Jesus speaks of destroying the temple and raising it in three days, and John explains that He meant the temple of His body. The statement of Revelation 21:22, that the Lord God and the Lamb are the temple, rests on this, since the true meeting place of God and humanity has always been in Him.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens in a garden and closes in a city, and this passage shows that the second is the fulfilment of the first and not a replacement. Genesis 2 gave a river, a tree, gold and gemstones in the land of Havilah, and a man set in the garden to work and keep it. Revelation 22 returns each of those pieces in a larger form: the river, the tree, the gold and the gems, and a people who serve and reign. The creation mandate has not been cancelled. It has been taken up into the life of a city, in which the nations bring their glory in 21:26.

The fall had closed the way with cherubim and a whirling sword, and the story that follows is about how a holy God could dwell again with sinful people. The answer unfolded in stages. A tent in the wilderness, a temple in Jerusalem, the Word made flesh, the church as a temple of the Spirit, and now the whole city as a Holy of Holies. At each stage the room grew larger and the barrier thinner, until in 21:22 there is no temple, because God and the Lamb are the temple. The sentence of Genesis 3 is answered by 22:3, 'No longer will there be any curse.'

The passage also gathers the story of the two cities. Cain built a city, Babel built a city, and Babylon filled the earth with its wealth until it fell. Abraham waited for a city with foundations, Hebrews 11:10, and this is it. The human desire for a place to belong and a name to carry is not condemned but fulfilled, once the builder is God.

It sets up the closing words of the book. The angel who showed the city will say in 22:6 that these words are faithful and true, and the invitation of 22:17, 'Come,' is addressed to the thirsty outside it. The story ends as a promise held open, and the reader is invited to step in through the gate, wash the robe and drink from the river that runs from the throne.

In that city the face of God is seen, and the old curse and the old night are gone. It is the end toward which the whole Bible was written, and the passage leaves the reader with the picture of God and the Lamb at the centre of the street, and the nations walking in the light.

sermon.title: The New Jerusalem
sermon.why: Preached in the series Revelation: The Final Word on exactly this passage, Revelation 21:1-22:5, Keller unfolds the descending bride city and its restoration of Eden as the church's certain future hope of death conquered and all things restored.

quiz.q: Why does John see no temple in the New Jerusalem, Revelation 21:22?

options.text: Because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are themselves its temple.
options.note: This is stated directly in verse 22.

options.text: Because the city was too small to contain a temple building.
options.note: The reason given is theological, God and the Lamb are the temple, not a matter of size.

options.text: Because worship has ended entirely in the new creation.
options.note: Worship continues unbroken, Revelation 22:3, it simply needs no separate building.

options.text: Because the city belongs only to angels, not to redeemed people.
options.note: The city is the dwelling of God's redeemed people, His servants who worship Him there.

quiz.q: What does the city's cube shape, 12,000 stadia in every direction, most likely recall?

options.text: The Holy of Holies, the cube-shaped Most Holy Place of Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 6:20.
options.note: Many interpreters read the cube as identifying the whole city with the innermost sanctuary.

options.text: A literal city plan with no symbolic significance at all.
options.note: Even readers who take the numbers literally recognize the deliberate echo of the Holy of Holies' shape.

options.text: The size of ancient Rome, which the city is meant to outmatch.
options.note: The shape's significance lies in temple imagery, not a comparison to Rome's dimensions.

options.text: Nothing in particular; cube shapes have no meaning in Scripture.
options.note: The Most Holy Place was built as a cube, making the echo unmistakable.

quiz.q: What is significant about the twelve gates named for the tribes and the twelve foundations named for the apostles?

options.text: They join the Old and New Covenant people of God into one city, one people.
options.note: Israel's tribes and the Lamb's apostles together form the city's structure.

options.text: They show that only Israel, not the church, will dwell in the city.
options.note: Both tribes and apostles are named together, uniting rather than excluding either group.

options.text: They are decorative details with no connection to God's people.
options.note: The names directly identify God's covenant people across both testaments.

options.text: They indicate exactly twenty-four literal individuals will live there.
options.note: The names represent the whole believing community of both covenants, not a headcount.

quiz.q: What flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb in Revelation 22:1-2?

options.text: A river of the water of life, with the tree of life growing on both its banks.
options.note: This matches the vision exactly.

options.text: A river of fire consuming the unrighteous.
options.note: That is a different image found elsewhere in Revelation; here the river is the water of life, a picture of blessing.

options.text: A road leading out of the city toward the nations.
options.note: The text describes a river and a tree, not a road.

options.text: Nothing; the throne is described as dry and empty.
options.note: The throne is the very source of the river of life.

quiz.q: What does 'no longer will there be any curse,' Revelation 22:3, mean for God's people?

options.text: The curse placed on the ground and on humanity after the fall, Genesis 3:17-19, is fully reversed.
options.note: This directly answers the judgments of Genesis 3.

options.text: Only physical illness will end, while spiritual separation from God continues.
options.note: The removal of the curse includes unbroken worship and seeing God's face, not physical healing alone.

options.text: Some believers will still live under partial judgment.
options.note: The text states no curse will remain at all for God's people in the city.

options.text: The curse simply moves from the earth to the New Jerusalem.
options.note: The city is precisely where the curse is declared absent.

questions: The bride, the holy city, is shown as radiant with the very glory of God. What would it look like for you to let that future glory shape how you see your present, ordinary life?
There is no temple because God and the Lamb are the temple, no more distance between His people and Himself. Where do you still feel distant from God, and how does this vision speak to that?
The tree of life, once barred in Eden, now stands open on both sides of the river. What does it mean to you that access to life with God is now a gift freely given, not a barrier to overcome?
'No longer will there be any curse.' What burden, brokenness, or grief in your life right now most needs to hear that promise?
God's people will see His face and reign with Him forever. How does that future hope change the way you face this week's disappointments or delays?

translationNotes.note: 12,000 stadia and 144 cubits are both built from the number twelve, twelve squared multiplied by a thousand, and twelve times twelve, numbers that saturate the vision with the completeness of God's covenant people rather than functioning as an ordinary architect's plan.

Jasper here is likely a clear or translucent stone rather than the opaque stone known by that name today, since it is repeatedly compared to crystal and glass; ancient stone names did not always match modern mineral classifications.
The Lamb's Book of Life was introduced earlier in Revelation, 13:8 and 20:12, 15; its mention here ties this vision of the city's purity to the final judgment scene that precedes it.

'The leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations' does not imply sickness remains in the new creation; it pictures the tree's abundance as continual life and flourishing for all peoples, not a remedy for ongoing disease.

meta.notes: BSB text supplied and pre-verified this session; Poetic line breaks were already flattened into flowing prose as supplied, and straight quotation marks were converted to curly typographic marks with no change to wording. The passage spans two chapters; the chapter field in the verses array correctly reads 21 for verses 9 through 27 and switches to 22 for verses 1 through 5, with the switch occurring precisely between Revelation 21:27 and 22:1 as required.
